Delightful: Aristotle’s refutation of “need” as the driving force behind power, Book II, Chapter V (p. 33, Stahr):
“One does not become a tyrant in order not to be cold—τυραννοῦσιν οὐχ ἵνα μὴ ῥιγῶσιν.”
If I have no power, I will be devoured. But there is already the old story: they go hungry when they do not have power.
The three-hundredth anniversary celebration of Leviathan in Frankfurt, with Alfred Andersch, Nicolaus Sombart, Anima, Hannes and Freda Winckelmann, Hausenstein.
Andersch strongly emphasized and repeatedly affirmed his belief in human free will.
When you speak of free will, you fall into the standard formulas and dead ends of academic philosophy.
You mean something completely different from determinism or indeterminism.
You mean something every decent human being does.
Something you and I have always done: when we fell in love, when we became politically passionate, when we threw ourselves wholeheartedly into something.
In truth, that was not free will. It was a blindes Vorgebot: a blind first commitment.
That is the word. And with the word, we have the thing itself and the situation itself: the blind first commitment.
Even more important than the questions on the questionnaires are the great central questions that “they”—that is, Roosevelt and Stalin acting as a single coalition!—put to the Germans in 1945.
So answer, for example, the following:
Do you consider Thomas Mann or Heinrich Mann the greatest German poet?
Do you consider Heinrich Heine or Zuckmayer the true spokesman of your generation?
Do you consider Robert Kempner or Erich Kaufmann the true representatives of the German sense of law and justice?
To every question of this kind I answer firmly:
Monarchical-dynastic legitimacy ends in disputes over family law, wars of succession, and harassment over family trees.

Democratic legitimacy ends in the sordid tricks of electoral law and in arguments over proportional representation, electoral districts, and the calculation of that mysterious quantity called “the majority.”

Haec omnis, quam cernis, inops inhumataque turba est.
“This whole crowd you see is destitute and unburied.”
A destitute, unburied crowd. They are no longer buried.
Their bodies are burned. For a while they believed that they voluntarily “had themselves” cremated. That was the brief transitional stage of a liberal illusion.
That is a definition of the mass.
The transformation of people into a mass begins with the abolition of burial.
Etenim sacramentum regis abscondere bonum est.

I was just about to become annoyed when I read about the great academic honor that the University of Maryland (!) had bestowed, pari passu, on Cloy and Heuss and Friesenhahn.
Then I happened upon Hobbes, De Cive, Chapter X, p. 177 of the 1648 edition:
“To see the judgment of someone we despise preferred to our own;
to see our own wisdom disregarded before our very eyes;
in the uncertain contest for empty glory, to incur the most certain of enmities—for this cannot be avoided whether we win or lose;
to hate and be hated because our opinions differ;
to expose our plans and wishes to everyone when there is no need to do so, and gain nothing from it;
to neglect our private affairs—these are evils.”
But being excluded from having a say is not one of them.
O Wisdom, you speak like old Hobbes!
You continue the catalogue in Hamlet’s monologue:
All you have to do is open your ears.
All you have to do is listen. For example, I hear the word Staatsroman—“state-novel”—used for utopia.
Robert von Mohl came up with it.
Staatsräson—reason of state—is only one side of the state. The Staatsroman—the state-novel—is the other. The state becomes the realm of the pure novel.
Today’s written constitutions are state-novels of this kind. They begin with the sentence:
“All Germans are equal before the law.”
A beautiful opening sentence for a novel.
Better to leave the rest unwritten.
It would not win the Nobel Prize anyway.

I remember the wonderful conversations with Tierno and Truyol about the dead point that must arise in every relationship of mutual exchange unless there is a blind first commitment and a blind advance performance.
According to Hobbes (De Cive, Chapter II, §18), this dead point is overcome sola fide—by faith alone.
So there we have sola fides inside legal theory!
I maintain that it can be overcome only by the blind first commitment. That is human freedom.
“Ubi vero creditur”—where there is trust—the contractus, the contract, grows out of the pactum, the agreement.
Credit—trust—is the essence of the pactum. It follows that the foundation of constitutional law is a situation of trust, which means: peace.
The principle pacta sunt servanda—agreements must be kept—is only the second principle of law. It is not the foundation. The foundation is peace. That is: a situation.
Law through peace is meaningful and decent.
Peace through law is an imperialist claim to rule.
Between you and us, on both sides, lie too many desecrated bodies.
The burning of the men hanged at Nuremberg made this condition even worse.
Now they cannot even be buried after the fact.
Rhyme is to verse what color is to painting.
Human beings do not see light. They see color.
The German classical writers had a deeply inadequate relationship to color and to painting.
Today we experience color as an element in itself.
Its power to create space is stronger than the illusion of space created by any linear perspective. We experience Paul Klee as an entirely new world.
If that is so, then we will also come to understand rhyme as an element in itself.
Its first eruption came during the First World War.
